query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) develop and retain a protective oxide layer at high temperatures because their inherently high configurational entropy forces a uniform distribution and limited diffusion of reactive elements (such as Al or Cr), enabling selective oxidation that forms a continuous, adherent, and slow‐growing oxide scale. In other words, the multicomponent mixture kinetically limits further oxidation and spallation by establishing a self-healing barrier.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy formulated with multiple principal elements including minor amounts of oxidation-prone elements (e.g., Al and/or Cr), prepared with a homogeneous microstructure, and a baseline conventional alloy of similar major components but lacking high configurational entropy.
generation.intervention: Expose both the HEA and the conventional alloy (baseline) to controlled high-temperature oxidation conditions.
generation.conditions: Samples are subjected to isothermal oxidation in an oxygen-rich atmosphere (e.g., air) at temperatures between 800°C and 1000°C for a fixed period.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous protective oxide scale (e.g., Al2O3 or Cr2O3) at the alloy surface; its adherence and slow growth are mediated by the limited interdiffusion enabled by the high entropy of the alloy.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy in the HEA creates a thermodynamically stabilized, uniformly distributed pool of reactive elements. Under high-temperature oxidation, these elements preferentially form a compact oxide, while the sluggish diffusion kinetics inherent to the multicomponent system limit further oxidation and prevent scale spallation. In contrast, conventional alloys, with less entropy stabilization, have less uniform reactive element distribution and faster diffusion, leading to thicker, less adherent oxides.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline conventional alloy, the HEA is expected to develop a thinner, more uniform, and better-adhering oxide layer with slower growth kinetics during high-temperature exposure, thereby providing superior oxidation resistance.
generation.baseline: A conventional single-phase alloy having a similar primary composition but lacking the multicomponent, high configurational entropy character.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be operative under high-temperature, oxidizing environments (800–1000°C) in oxygen-rich atmospheres. It may not apply if the alloy composition lacks sufficient reactive elements to form a protective oxide phase or if temperatures exceed thresholds that lead to scale spallation irrespective of diffusion kinetics.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the relative contributions of specific reactive elements (e.g., the roles of Al versus Cr) and the precise kinetics of oxide scale formation in different HEA systems. The universality across all HEAs for high-temperature oxidation resistance also requires further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sample sets: one high-entropy alloy containing multiple principal elements with minor additions of oxidation-promoting elements (e.g., Al and/or Cr) and a conventional alloy that has the major elements but in a less complex (low-entropy) configuration. Subject both sets to identical isothermal oxidation treatments at 900°C in air over a specified duration. Compare the oxide layer characteristics of both alloys.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and uniformity via cross-sectional SEM
Surface composition and phase analysis via XPS/EDS
Weight gain measurements over time to assess oxidation kinetics
Adhesion testing (e.g., spallation or scratch tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA does not display a statistically significant improvement over the conventional alloy in forming a thinner, more uniform, and more adherent oxide scale (i.e., if both materials exhibit similar oxidation kinetics and oxide characteristics), then the hypothesis that high configurational entropy governs the ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer will be falsified.

Microstructure and Composition Evolution of a Fused Slurry Silicide Coating on MoNbTaTiW Refractory High-Entropy Alloy in High-Temperature Oxidation Environment

Abstract: AbstractIn this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M5Si3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness.
